Leveraging this fine-grained model, we introduce Differentiated Bi-Directional Intervention (DBDI), a new white-box framework that precisely neutralizes the safety alignment at critical layer. DBDI applies adaptive projection nullification to the refusal execution direction while suppressing the harm detection direction via direct steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DBDI outperforms prominent jailbreaking methods, achieving up to a 97.88\% attack success rate on models such as Llama-2. By providing a more granular and mechanistic framework, our work offers a new direction for the in-depth understanding of LLM safety alignment.

papers.title: ConceptGuard: Neuro-Symbolic Safety Guardrails via Sparse Interpretable Jailbreak Concepts
papers.research_question: Can SAEs disentangle dense LLM activations into sparse, interpretable concepts representing jailbreak-related themes? Can these concepts facilitate interpretable, concept-guided guardrails that generalize across diverse jailbreak styles while preserving model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ConceptGuard, a framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders to extract interpretable jailbreak concepts from LLM activations and builds a linear guardrail that generalizes to stealthy jailbreaks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ConceptGuard demonstrates that interpretable jailbreak concepts can be extracted from LLM activations using SAEs and used to build a linear guardrail that generalizes across jailbreak styles without fine-tuning, offering a robust and transparent safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can disentangle dense LLM activations into sparse, interpretable concepts corresponding to jailbreak themes.
The concept-guided guardrail (trained only on base attacks) generalizes to stealthy jailbreak styles (e.g., hypothetical, BoN) without exposure to them during training.
The pruned guardrail (using only rich features) reduces the feature space by 57% while maintaining competitive performance.
The guardrail outperforms baseline safety-tuned models (like Llama-Guard) in generalization.
The activation-based guardrails are robust to input perturbations that confuse the model, as shown by UMAP visualizations.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a single hook point (attention layer of the 8th transformer block).
The pruning heuristic might be overly aggressive and classify safety-critical features as junk.
The method assumes the model has undergone safety fine-tuning; effectiveness on unaligned models is unknown.
The linear classifier may not capture complex, non-linear interactions between jailbreak concepts.
future_direction: Using sparse-crosscoders to extract interacting harmful concepts across multiple layers.
Exploring more sophisticated methods to identify safety-critical features without relying strictly on token-level interpretability metrics.
Testing the method on unaligned foundational models and exploring more expressive classifiers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have found success in a variety of applications. However, their safety remains a concern due to the existence of various jailbreaking methods. Despite significant efforts, alignment and safety fine-tuning only provide a certain degree of robustness against jailbreak attacks that covertly mislead LLMs towards the generation of harmful content. This leaves them prone to a range of vulnerabilities, including targeted misuse and accidental user profiling. This work introduces \textbf{ConceptGuard}, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify interpretable concepts within LLM internals associated with different jailbreak themes. By extracting semantically meaningful internal representations, ConceptGuard enables building robust safety guardrails -- offering fully explainable and generalizable defenses without sacrificing model capabilities or requiring further fine-tuning. Leveraging advances in the mechanistic interpretability of LLMs, our approach provides evidence for a shared activation geometry for jailbreak attacks in the representation space, a potential foundation for designing more interpretable and generalizable safeguards against attackers.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs via Attention Distribution Modeling
papers.research_question: How can concept learning models achieve domain-invariant concepts that generalize across domains while maintaining consistency within classes (concept fidelity and interoperability)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a self-explaining neural architecture that improves concept fidelity and interoperability across domains by incorporating a salient concept selection network, contrastive learning for domain invariance, and prototype-based concept grounding.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully learns domain-invariant concepts, improving concept interoperability and fidelity, and demonstrates efficacy through empirical results on domain adaptation tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method (RCE+PCG+CCL) outperforms existing self-explaining concept learning baselines in domain adaptation performance across multiple datasets.
Each component (RCE, PCG, CCL) contributes to improved performance, as shown in ablation studies.
The method achieves higher concept fidelity scores, indicating more consistent concepts within classes.
Qualitative visualizations show that the learned concepts are domain-aligned and can explain samples from both source and target domains.
papers.abstract: Most jailbreak methods for large language models (LLMs) focus on superficially improving attack success through manually defined rules. However, they fail to uncover the underlying mechanisms within target LLMs that explain why an attack succeeds or fails. In this paper, we propose investigating the phenomenon of jailbreaks and defenses for LLMs from the perspective of attention distributions within the models. A preliminary experiment reveals that the success of a jailbreak is closely linked to the LLM's attention on sensitive words.Inspired by this interesting finding, we propose incorporating critical signals derived from internal attention distributions within LLMs, namely Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words and Attention Dispersion Entropy, to guide both attacks and defenses. Drawing inspiration from the concept of "Feint and Attack", we introduce an attention-guided jailbreak model, ABA, which redirects the model's attention to benign contexts, and an attention-based defense model, ABD, designed to detect attacks by analyzing internal attention entropy. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposal when compared to SOTA baselines.

papers.title: SafeInt: Shielding Large Language Models from Jailbreak Attacks via Safety-Aware Representation Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we defend large language models against jailbreak attacks by intervening in their internal representations to relocate jailbreak-related representations into the rejection region?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SafeIntervention (SafeInt), a defense method that adaptively intervenes in jailbreak-related representations to align them with unsafe sample representations, thereby activating the model's refusal mechanisms while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeInt, a representation intervention-based defense, effectively shields LLMs from jailbreak attacks by adaptively relocating jailbreak representations into the rejection region, outperforming existing methods while preserving model utility.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of jailbreak samples are distinguishable from safe and unsafe samples in intermediate and later layers of LLMs.
Representation distributions of different jailbreak methods (e.g., GCG, AutoDAN, DeepInception) are consistent, especially in intermediate layers.
SafeInt outperforms all baseline defense methods in reducing Attack Success Rate (ASR) across various jailbreak attacks and datasets.
SafeInt maintains utility (measured by MT-Bench and Just-Eval) close to the non-defended model, often better than other defenses.
SafeInt remains effective against adaptive attacks and real-time jailbreak attempts.
papers.limitation: The transferability of SafeInt to different but homologous LLMs has not been explored in depth.
papers.abstract: With the widespread real-world deployment of large language models (LLMs), ensuring their behavior complies with safety standards has become crucial. Jailbreak attacks exploit vulnerabilities in LLMs to induce undesirable behavior, posing a significant threat to LLM safety. Previous defenses often fail to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency simultaneously. Defenses from a representation perspective offer new insights, but existing interventions cannot dynamically adjust representations based on the harmfulness of the queries. To address this limitation, we propose SafeIntervention (SafeInt), a novel defense method that shields LLMs from jailbreak attacks through safety-aware representation intervention. Built on our analysis of the representations of jailbreak samples, the core idea of SafeInt is to relocate jailbreak-related representations into the rejection region. This is achieved by intervening in the representation distributions of jailbreak samples to align them with those of unsafe samples. We conduct comprehensive experiments covering six jailbreak attacks, two jailbreak datasets, and two utility benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that SafeInt outperforms all baselines in defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks while largely maintaining utility. Additionally, we evaluate SafeInt against adaptive attacks and verify its effectiveness in mitigating real-time attacks.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Exploits with Responsible AI Considerations
papers.research_question: How can we defend large language models against jailbreak exploits? The paper proposes and evaluates three defense strategies.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of jailbreak defenses and three defense strategies (prompt-level, logit-based steering, and domain-specific agent) that reduce attack success rates, with the agent-based defense achieving full mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that jailbreaks pose significant risks and that targeted interventions can prevent them, but defenses involve trade-offs between safety, computational efficiency, and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
The prompt-level defense reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) by about 22% for aligned models and 8% for unaligned models.
The logit-based steering defense reduces ASR by 18% for aligned models and 43% for unaligned models.
The domain-specific agent defense (using MetaGPT) achieves zero ASR, fully mitigating jailbreak attempts.
Aligned models (with training-time defenses) show lower baseline ASR and are more robust to jailbreaks.
Defense strategies involve trade-offs between safety, computational efficiency, and scalability.
papers.limitation:
Defense strategies often involve trade-offs between safety, performance, and scalability.
The domain-specific agent defense incurs higher computational cost and latency due to multiple inference passes.
future_direction: Explore adaptive and efficient defense mechanisms that maintain both robustness and usability in real-world LLM applications.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain susceptible to jailbreak exploits that bypass safety filters and induce harmful or unethical behavior. This work presents a systematic taxonomy of existing jailbreak defenses across prompt-level, model-level, and training-time interventions, followed by three proposed defense strategies. First, a Prompt-Level Defense Framework detects and neutralizes adversarial inputs through sanitization, paraphrasing, and adaptive system guarding. Second, a Logit-Based Steering Defense reinforces refusal behavior through inference-time vector steering in safety-sensitive layers. Third, a Domain-Specific Agent Defense employs the MetaGPT framework to enforce structured, role-based collaboration and domain adherence. Experiments on benchmark datasets show substantial reductions in attack success rate, achieving full mitigation under the agent-based defense. Overall, this study highlights how jailbreaks pose a significant security threat to LLMs and identifies key intervention points for prevention, while noting that defense strategies often involve trade-offs between safety, performance, and scalability. Code is available at: https://github.com/Kuro0911/CS5446-Project

papers.title: PII Jailbreaking in LLMs via Activation Steering Reveals Personal Information Leakage
papers.research_question: Can aligned LLMs be steered to produce non-refusal responses to privacy-sensitive prompts? Do the resulting responses disclose factual personal information or merely hallucinate?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can jailbreak aligned LLMs to bypass refusal mechanisms and disclose factual personal information, highlighting privacy risks from memorized data.
papers.conclusion: Privacy-related prompts combined with targeted steering provide a stress test for assessing the extent to which LLMs memorize and reveal personal information.
papers.key_findings:
Attention head activations can reliably predict model's refusal behavior for privacy-sensitive prompts.
Steering top-k attention heads induces non-refusal responses to privacy queries.
Steered responses frequently contain factual personal information, such as relationships and life events.
Jailbreaking success rates exceed 80% across multiple LLMs with steering.
Factuality rates of disclosed information are high, indicating real privacy leakage.
papers.limitation:
Factual accuracy of steered responses is assessed using GPT-4, which may introduce evaluation errors.
Analysis is restricted to a single private attribute (sexual orientation).
Disagreements among human annotators when labeling responses as disclosed, due to subjective interpretation.
future_direction: Developing more robust fact-checking agents with web access to independently verify factual claims.
Extending the framework to other sensitive and verifiable attributes such as health conditions or financial status.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates privacy jailbreaking in LLMs via steering, focusing on whether manipulating activations can bypass LLM alignment and alter response behaviors to privacy related queries (e.g., a certain public figure's sexual orientation). We begin by identifying attention heads predictive of refusal behavior for private attributes (e.g., sexual orientation) using lightweight linear probes trained with privacy evaluator labels. Next, we steer the activations of a small subset of these attention heads guided by the trained probes to induce the model to generate non-refusal responses. Our experiments show that these steered responses often disclose sensitive attribute details, along with other private information about data subjects such as life events, relationships, and personal histories that the models would typically refuse to produce. Evaluations across four LLMs reveal jailbreaking disclosure rates of at least 95%, with more than 50% on average of these responses revealing true personal information. Our controlled study demonstrates that private information memorized in LLMs can be extracted through targeted manipulation of internal activations.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
papers.research_question: Do LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate concepts internally, and how can this separation be analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately in their internal representations, and the harmfulness direction extracted at the instruction token can be used to manipulate and analyze model safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately, providing a new dimension for understanding and improving AI safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Harmfulness is encoded at the last token of the user instruction (t_inst), while refusal is encoded at the last token of the post-instruction tokens (t_post-inst).
Steering along the harmfulness direction can cause LLMs to reinterpret harmless inputs as harmful, while steering along the refusal direction only reinforces refusal behavior without changing harmfulness judgment.
Jailbreak methods often work by suppressing refusal signals without altering the model's internal belief that the instruction is harmful.
Harmfulness representations are fine-grained and vary across risk categories, whereas refusal directions are similar across categories.
The latent harmfulness representation can be used to build an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) that performs comparably to finetuned safety models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not investigate the role of different layers in formulating refusal and harmfulness.
Experiments are limited to 7B and 8B models, so findings may not generalize to larger models.
future_direction: Study the role of each layer in harmfulness and refusal representations.
Investigate how harmfulness and refusal encoding changes with model size.
Use circuit analysis to understand the relation between internal harmfulness belief and external refusal behavior.
papers.abstract: LLMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions, but do they truly understand harmfulness beyond just refusing? Prior work has shown that LLMs' refusal behaviors can be mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, i.e., a refusal direction. In this work, we identify a new dimension to analyze safety mechanisms in LLMs, i.e., harmfulness, which is encoded internally as a separate concept from refusal. There exists a harmfulness direction that is distinct from the refusal direction. As causal evidence, steering along the harmfulness direction can lead LLMs to interpret harmless instructions as harmful, but steering along the refusal direction tends to elicit refusal responses directly without reversing the model's judgment on harmfulness. Furthermore, using our identified harmfulness concept, we find that certain jailbreak methods work by reducing the refusal signals without reversing the model's internal belief of harmfulness. We also find that adversarially finetuning models to accept harmful instructions has minimal impact on the model's internal belief of harmfulness. These insights lead to a practical safety application: The model's latent harmfulness representation can serve as an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) for detecting unsafe inputs and reducing over-refusals that is robust to finetuning attacks. For instance, our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods. Our findings suggest that LLMs' internal understanding of harmfulness is more robust than their refusal decision to diverse input instructions, offering a new perspective to study AI safety.

papers.title: Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations
papers.research_question: Why does jailbreak transferability occur? Is it due to shared representations or incidental flaws?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak transferability emerges from shared representations, and increasing representational similarity through benign-only distillation causally increases transfer.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak transfer is reframed as a consequence of representation alignment rather than an incidental byproduct of safety training.
papers.key_findings:
Representational similarity and jailbreak strength on the source model are two factors that systematically shape transferability.
Distilling a target model on benign data from a source model increases their representational similarity and causally increases jailbreak transferability.
Persona-style jailbreaks transfer more reliably than cipher-based jailbreaks, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit shared representation space.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak transferability is the surprising phenomenon when an adversarial attack compromising one model also elicits harmful responses from other models. Despite widespread demonstrations, there is little consensus on why transfer is possible: is it a quirk of safety training, an artifact of model families, or a more fundamental property of representation learning? We present evidence that transferability emerges from shared representations rather than incidental flaws. Across 20 open-weight models and 33 jailbreak attacks, we find two factors that systematically shape transfer: (1) representational similarity under benign prompts, and (2) the strength of the jailbreak on the source model. To move beyond correlation, we show that deliberately increasing similarity through benign only distillation causally increases transfer. Our qualitative analyses reveal systematic transferability patterns across different types of jailbreaks. For example, persona-style jailbreaks transfer far more often than cipher-based prompts, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit models' shared representation space, whereas cipher-based attacks rely on idiosyncratic quirks that do not generalize. Together, these results reframe jailbreak transfer as a consequence of representation alignment rather than a fragile byproduct of safety training.

papers.title: Do Internal Layers of LLMs Reveal Patterns for Jailbreak Detection?
papers.research_question: Do internal layers of LLMs reveal patterns for jailbreak detection? Specifically, how do hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that analyzing internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts.
papers.conclusion: Examining internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition techniques provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts, offering a simple, efficient, and effective pathway for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
For GPT-J, Multi-Head Attention (MHA) representations outperform layer outputs for jailbreak classification.
For Mamba-2, Mixer representations outperform Block outputs for jailbreak classification.
Tensor decomposition of internal representations yields latent factors that provide clear separation between jailbreak and benign prompts.
A simple pipeline of tensor decomposition followed by basic classifiers (e.g., Random Forest, SVM) achieves effective jailbreak detection.
papers.limitation: The study is preliminary and requires further work on larger datasets, additional architectures, and more sophisticated evaluation settings.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to larger datasets.
Apply the methodology to additional architectures.
Conduct more sophisticated evaluation.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a pressing concern with the increasing prevalence and accessibility of conversational LLMs. Adversarial users often exploit these models through carefully engineered prompts to elicit restricted or sensitive outputs, a strategy widely referred to as jailbreaking. While numerous defense mechanisms have been proposed, attackers continuously develop novel prompting techniques, and no existing model can be considered fully resistant. In this study, we investigate the jailbreak phenomenon by examining the internal representations of LLMs, with a focus on how hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts. Specifically, we analyze the open-source LLM GPT-J and the state-space model Mamba2, presenting preliminary findings that highlight distinct layer-wise behaviors. Our results suggest promising directions for further research on leveraging internal model dynamics for robust jailbreak detection and defense.

papers.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
papers.research_question: How different are the refusal directions when computed for different types of refusal behavior beyond safety, and how do these directions get expressed in the latent space such that they facilitate various styles of refusal under a similar intervention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal behavior in LLMs is mediated by multiple geometrically distinct activation-space directions, but linear steering along any refusal-related direction acts as a one-dimensional control knob for refusal, with differences primarily in refusal style. Sparse autoencoders reveal a structured internal representation with a shared core of refusal latents and a long tail of style-specific latents.
papers.conclusion: The internal structure of refusal is rich and structured, but linear control flattens this complexity, highlighting the limits of linear interpretability for aligned model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Different refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space.
Linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal–over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob.
The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses (style).
Sparse autoencoders uncover a structured internal representation: a small reusable core of shared refusal latents supplemented by a long tail of style- and domain-specific latents.
Linear interventions collapse over this structure, flattening mechanistic differences into uniform behavioral control.
papers.limitation:
The techniques could be misused to suppress refusal behavior and facilitate the generation of harmful content.
Linear steering collapses a rich internal refusal structure into a coarse behavioral knob, underscoring that such interventions are not suitable as principled safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Prior work argues that refusal in large language models is mediated by a single activation-space direction, enabling effective steering and ablation. We show that this account is incomplete. Across eleven categories of refusal and non-compliance, including safety, incomplete or unsupported requests, anthropomorphization, and over-refusal, we find that these refusal behaviors correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space. Yet despite this diversity, linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal to over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob. The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses.

papers.title: Bleeding Pathways: Vanishing Discriminability in LLM Hidden States Fuels Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the inherent immunity of conventionally aligned LLMs against existing jailbreak attacks without significantly sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DEEPALIGN, a fine-tuning method that uses contrastive hidden-state steering to enhance LLM safety by amplifying the separation between harmful and benign hidden states during generation, reducing jailbreak success while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: DEEPALIGN provides a unified, architecture-agnostic defense that significantly improves the safety-utility Pareto frontier by enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention during generation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs' capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates as generation progresses, reflected in diminishing separability of hidden states.
DEEPALIGN reduces attack success rates of diverse jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal levels across multiple LLMs.
DEEPALIGN preserves model utility and reduces over-refusal compared to baseline defenses.
The method's automated data generation diversifies safe response patterns, increasing resilience against attacks targeting limited refusal patterns.
DEEPALIGN maintains robustness against an adaptive attack derived from DrAttack.
papers.limitation: The adaptive attack presents a challenge by providing the model with a malicious yet seemingly benign response prefix, testing robustness against adversarial out-of-distribution prefixes.
papers.abstract: LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit adversarial prompts to circumvent safety measures. Current safety fine-tuning approaches face two critical limitations. First, they often fail to strike a balance between security and utility, where stronger safety measures tend to over-reject harmless user requests. Second, they frequently miss malicious intent concealed within seemingly benign tasks, leaving models exposed to exploitation. Our work identifies a fundamental cause of these issues: during response generation, an LLM's capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates. Experimental evidence confirms this, revealing that the separability between hidden states for safe and harmful responses diminishes as generation progresses. This weakening discrimination forces models to make compliance judgments earlier in the generation process, restricting their ability to recognize developing harmful intent and contributing to both aforementioned failures. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduce DEEPALIGN - an inherent defense framework that enhances the safety of LLMs. By applying contrastive hidden-state steering at the midpoint of response generation, DEEPALIGN amplifies the separation between harmful and benign hidden states, enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention throughout the generation process. Across diverse LLMs spanning varying architectures and scales, it reduced attack success rates of nine distinct jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal. Crucially, it preserved model capability while reducing over-refusal. Models equipped with DEEPALIGN exhibited up to 3.5% lower error rates in rejecting challenging benign queries and maintained standard task performance with less than 1% decline. This marks a substantial advance in the safety-utility Pareto frontier.

papers.title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we balance safety and utility in large language models against jailbreak attacks by adjusting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Jailbreak Antidote, a method for real-time safety-utility balance by sparsely adjusting internal states during inference, showing that safety information is sparsely distributed and adjusting approximately 5% of the state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution for real-time safety adjustments in LLMs by directly manipulating internal states, enhancing safety while preserving utility and opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
Jailbreak Antidote achieves high defense success rates (DSR) across nine LLMs and ten jailbreak attack methods.
The method preserves model utility, maintaining high Win Rates on AlpacaEval while enhancing safety.
The approach is efficient, introducing negligible computational overhead and no additional token cost during inference.
The safety direction can be identified via PCA on hidden states from benign and harmful prompts.
papers.limitation:
The method requires pre-defined scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k; dynamically adapting these based on context or model confidence could improve flexibility.
Smaller models are inherently limited by their reduced parameter space, which may restrict the extent of safety adjustment.
Developing robust mechanisms to counter adversaries capable of explicitly exploiting the adjustments in internal states remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Dynamically adapting the scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k based on context or model confidence.
Addressing extreme adversarial settings where attackers explicitly exploit the internal state adjustments.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other aspects of model alignment, such as fairness or domain adaptation.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks, which manipulate LLMs into generating harmful content, pose significant challenges to this balance. Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
papers.research_question: How universal are refusal directions across languages? Specifically, does a refusal direction extracted from one language transfer to others?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages; a refusal vector extracted from one language can effectively modulate refusal behavior in other languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages, providing insights for multilingual safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
English-derived refusal vectors can jailbreak models across multiple languages.
Refusal vectors derived from any safety-aligned language (e.g., German, Chinese, Thai) transfer to other languages.
The universality is due to parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space.
Models fail to separate harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages, leading to vulnerabilities.
Adding refusal vectors can reduce compliance rates, demonstrating controllability.
papers.abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using PolyRefuse, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
The effect is observed across multiple models (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma) and is amplified by existing black-box jailbreak methods like CoP, PAIR, and TAP.
A preliminary safety-aware steering method (STEER-BIND) can partially mitigate the externality, suggesting a path for future safer steering techniques.
papers.limitation: t-SNE visualizations are qualitative projections and the 2D boundary is only an illustrative diagnostic.
future_direction: Develop safety-aware steering vectors (like STEER-BIND) that preserve robustness.
Include broader alignment evaluations (beyond safety refusal) when auditing steered models.
Routine red-teaming and regression testing of steered model configurations before deployment.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a practical post-training model alignment technique to enhance the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs). Prior to deploying a model as a service, developers can steer a pre-trained model toward specific behavioral objectives, such as compliance or instruction adherence, without the need for retraining. This process is as simple as adding a steering vector to the model's internal representations. However, this capability unintentionally introduces critical and under-explored safety risks. We identify a phenomenon termed Steering Externalities, where steering vectors derived from entirely benign datasets-such as those enforcing strict compliance or specific output formats like JSON-inadvertently erode safety guardrails. Experiments reveal that these interventions act as a force multiplier, creating new vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and increasing attack success rates to over 80% on standard benchmarks by bypassing the initial safety alignment. Ultimately, our results expose a critical blind spot in deployment: benign activation steering systematically erodes the "safety margin," rendering models more vulnerable to black-box attacks and proving that inference-time utility improvements must be rigorously audited for unintended safety externalities.

papers.title: Multi-Turn Jailbreaking Large Language Models via Attention Shifting
papers.research_question: What are the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreak attacks on LLMs, and how can attention shifting be leveraged to improve such attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ASJA, a multi-turn jailbreak method that shifts LLM attention away from harmful keywords by fabricating dialogue history using a genetic algorithm, achieving higher attack success rates and stealthiness.
papers.conclusion: ASJA effectively breaks the LLM's safety alignment by shifting attention to historical queries and responses via fabricated dialogue, outperforming baselines in effectiveness, stealthiness, and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
Successful multi-turn jailbreaks shift LLM attention away from harmful keywords to dialogue history, especially previous responses.
ASJA achieves higher attack success rates (44.91% improvement in harmfulness and 34.02% in relevance) compared to baselines.
ASJA maintains stealthiness (low perplexity) and has good transferability to other models.
The attention on harmful keywords in the last query is significantly lower in successful jailbreaks.
Optimizing both queries and responses in dialogue history is more effective than optimizing queries alone.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant performance in various natural language processing tasks but also pose safety and ethical threats, thus requiring red teaming and alignment processes to bolster their safety. To effectively exploit these aligned LLMs, recent studies have introduced jailbreak attacks based on multi-turn dialogues. These attacks aim to prompt LLMs to generate harmful or biased content by guiding them through contextual content. However, the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreaks remain unclear. Existing attacks often focus on optimizing queries and escalating toxicity to construct dialogues, lacking a thorough analysis of the inherent vulnerabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis of the differences between single-turn and multi-turn jailbreaks and find that successful multi-turn jailbreaks can effectively disperse the attention of LLMs on keywords associated with harmful behaviors, especially in historical responses. Based on this, we propose ASJA, a new multi-turn jailbreak approach by shifting the attention of LLMs, specifically by iteratively fabricating the dialogue history through a genetic algorithm to induce LLMs to generate harmful content. Extensive experiments on three LLMs and two datasets show that our approach surpasses existing approaches in jailbreak effectiveness, the stealth of jailbreak prompts, and attack efficiency. Our work emphasizes the importance of enhancing the robustness of LLMs' attention mechanism in multi-turn dialogue scenarios for a better defense strategy.

papers.title: Revisiting Jailbreaking for Large Language Models: A Representation Engineering Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms that make Large Language Models vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks, and are these linked to specific activation patterns in their representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'safety patterns' in LLMs' representation space that are crucial for self-safeguarding against malicious queries, and shows these patterns can be extracted and manipulated to control jailbreak vulnerability.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a new interpretation of jailbreaking through safety patterns, offering insights for attack and defense strategies, and raises concerns about the misuse of open-source LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Safety patterns can be extracted from LLMs using only a few contrastive query pairs.
Weakening safety patterns significantly reduces LLMs' self-safeguard capability, leading to successful jailbreaks.
Strengthening safety patterns enhances defense against stealthy jailbreak prompts.
Manipulating safety patterns has minimal impact on LLMs' general abilities and output quality.
Visualization analysis confirms that safety patterns affect the embedding distribution of malicious and benign inputs.
papers.limitation:
The findings are based on white-box settings, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Preventing misuse of safety pattern manipulation is a critical challenge.
future_direction: Exploring effective techniques such as Reverse Engineering based on the concept of safety patterns.
Developing comprehensive safeguarding strategies to ensure the safer use of LLMs, particularly in open-source models.
papers.abstract: The recent surge in jailbreaking attacks has revealed significant vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) when exposed to malicious inputs. While various defense strategies have been proposed to mitigate these threats, there has been limited research into the underlying mechanisms that make LLMs vulnerable to such attacks. In this study, we suggest that the self-safeguarding capability of LLMs is linked to specific activity patterns within their representation space. Although these patterns have little impact on the semantic content of the generated text, they play a crucial role in shaping LLM behavior under jailbreaking attacks. Our findings demonstrate that these patterns can be detected with just a few pairs of contrastive queries. Extensive experimentation shows that the robustness of LLMs against jailbreaking can be manipulated by weakening or strengthening these patterns. Further visual analysis provides additional evidence for our conclusions, providing new insights into the jailbreaking phenomenon. These findings highlight the importance of addressing the potential misuse of open-source LLMs within the community.

papers.title: A Causal Perspective for Enhancing Jailbreak Attack and Defense
papers.research_question: What are the causal relationships between interpretable prompt features and jailbreak occurrences in LLMs, and how can these be leveraged for attack and defense?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Causal Analyst, a framework that uses LLMs and causal discovery to identify direct causal features of jailbreaks, and demonstrates how these insights can boost attack success rates and improve defense via intent extraction.
papers.conclusion: Our results suggest that analyzing jailbreak features from a causal perspective is an effective and interpretable approach for improving LLM reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Specific prompt features like 'Positive Character' and 'Number of Task Steps' are direct causal drivers of jailbreaks.
The Jailbreaking Enhancer, which amplifies causal features, significantly increases attack success rates on various LLMs and benchmarks.
The Guardrail Advisor, leveraging the causal graph, effectively extracts true malicious intent from obfuscated queries, improving defense.
The causal analysis framework outperforms non-causal baselines in identifying jailbreak mechanisms.
The learned causal graphs are interpretable and provide actionable insights for both attack and defense.
papers.abstract: Uncovering the mechanisms behind "jailbreaks" in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their safety and reliability, yet these mechanisms remain poorly understood. Existing studies predominantly analyze jailbreak prompts by probing latent representations, often overlooking the causal relationships between interpretable prompt features and jailbreak occurrences. In this work, we propose Causal Analyst, a framework that integrates LLMs into data-driven causal discovery to identify the direct causes of jailbreaks and leverage them for both attack and defense. We introduce a comprehensive dataset comprising 35k jailbreak attempts across seven LLMs, systematically constructed from 100 attack templates and 50 harmful queries, annotated with 37 meticulously designed human-readable prompt features. By jointly training LLM-based prompt encoding and GNN-based causal graph learning, we reconstruct causal pathways linking prompt features to jailbreak responses. Our analysis reveals that specific features, such as "Positive Character" and "Number of Task Steps", act as direct causal drivers of jailbreaks. We demonstrate the practical utility of these insights through two applications: (1) a Jailbreaking Enhancer that targets identified causal features to significantly boost attack success rates on public benchmarks, and (2) a Guardrail Advisor that utilizes the learned causal graph to extract true malicious intent from obfuscated queries. Extensive experiments, including baseline comparisons and causal structure validation, confirm the robustness of our causal analysis and its superiority over non-causal approaches. Our results suggest that analyzing jailbreak features from a causal perspective is an effective and interpretable approach for improving LLM reliability. Our code is available at https://github.com/Master-PLC/Causal-Analyst.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: SOM Directions are Better than One: Multi-Directional Refusal Suppression in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is refusal behavior in language models better represented by a single linear direction or by a low-dimensional manifold of multiple directions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a multi-directional approach using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to model refusal as a manifold, showing that ablating multiple directions is more effective for refusal suppression than ablating a single direction.
papers.conclusion: Modeling refusal as a manifold spanned by multiple, closely related directions provides a more faithful and effective view of safety-related behaviors in LLMs than the single-direction perspective.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating multiple refusal directions identified by SOMs (MD) significantly outperforms the single-direction baseline (SD) and other jailbreak algorithms (GCG, SAA) in terms of Attack Success Rate (ASR).
Ablating multiple directions compresses the variance of harmful prompt representations and shifts them closer to harmless representations in the model's activation space.
The multiple directions extracted by SOMs are closely related (non-orthogonal), suggesting refusal is encoded as a manifold rather than a set of orthogonal components.
The method is effective even against a model with a defense mechanism (Mistral-7B-RR).
The effectiveness of refusal suppression generally increases with the number of ablated directions (k).
papers.limitation:
The Bayesian Optimization search for the best combination of directions can require a high number of trials as the search space grows, impacting scalability and speed.
The method computes directions at a single layer and applies ablation uniformly across all layers, potentially missing layer-specific variations in refusal encoding.
future_direction: Explore more efficient or structured search strategies, gradient-based optimization, or pruning algorithms to improve the scalability of the direction search.
Investigate layer-specific directions and ablation strategies to better capture refusal encoding across different layers.
Investigate the effectiveness of training separate SOMs for harmless prompts instead of using a single centroid.
papers.abstract: Refusal refers to the functional behavior enabling safety-aligned language models to reject harmful or unethical prompts. Following the growing scientific interest in mechanistic interpretability, recent work encoded refusal behavior as a single direction in the model's latent space; e.g., computed as the difference between the centroids of harmful and harmless prompt representations. However, emerging evidence suggests that concepts in LLMs often appear to be encoded as a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional latent space. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel method leveraging Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to extract multiple refusal directions. To this end, we first prove that SOMs generalize the prior work's difference-in-means technique. We then train SOMs on harmful prompt representations to identify multiple neurons. By subtracting the centroid of harmless representations from each neuron, we derive a set of multiple directions expressing the refusal concept. We validate our method on an extensive experimental setup, demonstrating that ablating multiple directions from models' internals outperforms not only the single-direction baseline but also specialized jailbreak algorithms, leading to an effective suppression of refusal. Finally, we conclude by analyzing the mechanistic implications of our approach.

papers.title: HSF: Defending against Jailbreak Attacks with Hidden State Filtering
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on LLMs by leveraging their hidden state representations to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before inference?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HSF, a plug-in defense module that uses hidden states from the last decoder layer to classify and block jailbreak attacks before inference, with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: HSF effectively defends against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks by leveraging the alignment capabilities reflected in LLM hidden states, offering an efficient and modular defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs can naturally distinguish between harmful, benign, and jailbreak queries within their hidden state representation space.
HSF significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) against six state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks while maintaining a low false positive rate.
HSF's defense performance is robust across different models (Llama2, Vicuna, Mistral) and requires only lightweight training of an added MLP classifier.
The method incurs negligible inference overhead and does not alter the core LLM architecture.
papers.limitation: Limited generalizability; HSF is tailored to specific LLMs and requires retraining when applied to other models.
future_direction: Explore how to leverage LLM hidden states to build more flexible harmful-behavior detectors.
Enhance jailbreak attack prevention through Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods.
papers.abstract: With the growing deployment of LLMs in daily applications like chatbots and content generation, efforts to ensure outputs align with human values and avoid harmful content have intensified. However, increasingly sophisticated jailbreak attacks threaten this alignment, aiming to induce unsafe outputs. Current defense efforts either focus on prompt rewriting or detection, which are limited in effectiveness due to the various design of jailbreak prompts, or on output control and detection, which are computationally expensive as they require LLM inference. Therefore, designing a pre-inference defense method that resists diverse jailbreak prompts is crucial for preventing LLM jailbreak attacks. We observe that jailbreak attacks, safe queries, and harmful queries exhibit different clustering patterns within the LLM's hidden state representation space. This suggests that by leveraging the LLM's hidden state representational capabilities, we can analyze the LLM's forthcoming behavior and proactively intervene for defense. In this paper, we propose a jailbreak attack defense strategy based on a Hidden State Filter (HSF), a lossless architectural defense mechanism that enables the model to preemptively identify and reject adversarial inputs before the inference process begins. We activate its defensive potential through an additional plugin module, effectively framing the defense task as a classification problem. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets, utilizing three different LLMs, show that HSF significantly enhances resilience against six cutting-edge jailbreak attacks. It significantly reduces the success rate of jailbreak attacks while minimally impacting responses to benign user queries, with negligible inference overhead, and outperforming defense baselines.Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Hidden-State-Filtering-8652/

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders are Capable LLM Jailbreak Mitigators
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be repurposed as effective jailbreak defenses? Does steering in sparse feature space offer advantages over dense activation space for jailbreak mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CC-Delta, an SAE-based jailbreak defense that uses context-conditioned feature selection and mean-shift steering in sparse latent space, showing better safety-utility tradeoffs and out-of-distribution generalization than dense-space methods.
papers.conclusion: Steering in sparse SAE feature space offers advantages over steering in dense activation space for jailbreak mitigation, and off-the-shelf SAEs can be repurposed as practical jailbreak defenses.
papers.key_findings:
CC-Delta achieves comparable or better safety-utility tradeoffs than baseline defenses across four models and twelve jailbreak attacks.
CC-Delta clearly outperforms dense mean-shift steering on all four models, particularly against out-of-distribution attacks.
Effective mitigation is highly sensitive to feature selection and often requires tens to hundreds of features.
The feature selection step (context-conditioned token selection and statistical ranking) is critical for maintaining utility.
Off-the-shelf SAEs trained for interpretability can be repurposed as practical jailbreak defenses without task-specific training.
papers.limitation:
Token matching requires the harmful request to appear verbatim in the jailbreak prompt, precluding application to re-writer attacks.
Auto-interpretability techniques have limitations in accurately labeling the behavior of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks remain a persistent threat to large language model safety. We propose Context-Conditioned Delta Steering (CC-Delta), an SAE-based defense that identifies jailbreak-relevant sparse features by comparing token-level representations of the same harmful request with and without jailbreak context. Using paired harmful/jailbreak prompts, CC-Delta selects features via statistical testing and applies inference-time mean-shift steering in SAE latent space. Across four aligned instruction-tuned models and twelve jailbreak attacks, CC-Delta achieves comparable or better safety-utility tradeoffs than baseline defenses operating in dense latent space. In particular, our method clearly outperforms dense mean-shift steering on all four models, and particularly against out-of-distribution attacks, showing that steering in sparse SAE feature space offers advantages over steering in dense activation space for jailbreak mitigation. Our results suggest off-the-shelf SAEs trained for interpretability can be repurposed as practical jailbreak defenses without task-specific training.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Attention-Based Strategies for Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the success of jailbreaks correlate with their influence on attention distributions within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided jailbreak attack (ABA) and an attention-based defense (ABD) by analyzing and manipulating attention distributions in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention distribution is a key factor in jailbreak attacks and defenses; the proposed ABA and ABD methods are effective in attacking and protecting LLMs, respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The success of a jailbreak attack is correlated with the model's attention on sensitive words; successful attacks divert attention away from harmful terms.
ABA achieves higher attack success rates (ASR-G >94%) than existing methods by minimizing attention on sensitive words and maximizing attention entropy.
ABD effectively defends against various jailbreak attacks by detecting anomalous attention distributions, achieving the lowest ASR-G in experiments.
The intention disguiser via attention-driven task nesting is a critical component for the success of ABA.
Excessive nesting layers in attack prompts can reduce effectiveness, with an optimal number around 3.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attack can be used to access the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by inducing LLMs to generate the harmful content. And the most common method of the attack is to construct semantically ambiguous prompts to confuse and mislead the LLMs. To access the security and reveal the intrinsic relation between the input prompt and the output for LLMs, the distribution of attention weight is introduced to analyze the underlying reasons. By using statistical analysis methods, some novel metrics are defined to better describe the distribution of attention weight, such as the Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words (Attn_SensWords), the Attention-based Contextual Dependency Score (Attn_DepScore) and Attention Dispersion Entropy (Attn_Entropy). By leveraging the distinct characteristics of these metrics, the beam search algorithm and inspired by the military strategy "Feint and Attack", an effective jailbreak attack strategy named as Attention-Based Attack (ABA) is proposed. In the ABA, nested attack prompts are employed to divert the attention distribution of the LLMs. In this manner, more harmless parts of the input can be used to attract the attention of the LLMs. In addition, motivated by ABA, an effective defense strategy called as Attention-Based Defense (ABD) is also put forward. Compared with ABA, the ABD can be used to enhance the robustness of LLMs by calibrating the attention distribution of the input prompt. Some comparative experiments have been given to demonstrate the effectiveness of ABA and ABD. Therefore, both ABA and ABD can be used to access the security of the LLMs. The comparative experiment results also give a logical explanation that the distribution of attention weight can bring great influence on the output for LLMs.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Model-Editing-Based Jailbreak against Safety-aligned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is there a more stealthy jailbreak attack vector for LLMs that minimizes user involvement by directly modifying internal model structures to bypass safety alignment without input modifications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Targeted Model Editing (TME), a white-box jailbreak method that bypasses safety filters by identifying and removing safety-critical transformations (SCTs) from MLP weight matrices, enabling harmful responses without input modifications while preserving normal model functionality.
papers.conclusion: The work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security via model editing-based jailbreaks and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations for unsafe samples are highly consistent (due to uniform refusal), while activations for safe samples are more variable.
The difference in average activation values between safe and unsafe samples is significantly larger than the variation within unsafe samples.
The overlap rate of activated neurons between safe and unsafe inputs is low (below 25%), indicating distinct processing pathways.
The D-LLM framework, which implements TME, achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% across four open-source LLMs.
The method maintains model performance on standard benchmarks (TruthfulQA, MMLU) after editing, showing preserved functionality.
future_direction: Further unveil the vulnerabilities of D-LLM and provide insights for LLM developers to bolster safety.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed numerous fields by enabling advanced natural language interactions but remain susceptible to critical vulnerabilities, particularly jailbreak attacks. Current jailbreak techniques, while effective, often depend on input modifications, making them detectable and limiting their stealth and scalability. This paper presents Targeted Model Editing (TME), a novel white-box approach that bypasses safety filters by minimally altering internal model structures while preserving the model's intended functionalities. TME identifies and removes safety-critical transformations (SCTs) embedded in model matrices, enabling malicious queries to bypass restrictions without input modifications. By analyzing distinct activation patterns between safe and unsafe queries, TME isolates and approximates SCTs through an optimization process. Implemented in the D-LLM framework, our method achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% on four mainstream open-source LLMs, maintaining high performance. Unlike existing methods, D-LLM eliminates the need for specific triggers or harmful response collections, offering a stealthier and more effective jailbreak strategy. This work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.

papers.title: Pruning for Protection: Increasing Jailbreak Resistance in Aligned LLMs Without Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How does model compression, specifically pruning, affect the jailbreak resistance of aligned large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Moderate pruning using WANDA increases jailbreak resistance in aligned LLMs without fine-tuning, while preserving performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning can improve jailbreak resistance in safety-trained LLMs, but excessive pruning reduces safety, suggesting that careful pruning can aid in deploying safe models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning at 10-30% sparsity improves jailbreak resistance, with peak improvement at 20% sparsity for LLaMA-2 Chat.
The degree of safety improvement correlates with the initial model's safety level; models with more safety training show greater improvement.
Pruned models exhibit sharper attention patterns and are less distracted by jailbreak pretexts.
Pruned models assign higher perplexity to jailbreak constructs, indicating increased sensitivity to out-of-distribution prompts.
Pruning enhances resistance against both manual jailbreak attempts and automated attacks like GCG.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 7-billion parameter models and WANDA pruning; results may not generalize to larger models or other compression techniques.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models
Explore other compression techniques beyond WANDA pruning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of model compression on the way Large Language Models (LLMs) process prompts, particularly concerning jailbreak resistance. We show that moderate WANDA pruning can enhance resistance to jailbreaking attacks without fine-tuning, while maintaining performance on standard benchmarks. To systematically evaluate this safety enhancement, we introduce a dataset of 225 harmful tasks across five categories. Our analysis of LLaMA-2 Chat, Vicuna 1.3, and Mistral Instruct v0.2 reveals that pruning benefits correlate with initial model safety levels. We interpret these results by examining changes in attention patterns and perplexity shifts, demonstrating that pruned models exhibit sharper attention and increased sensitivity to artificial jailbreak constructs. We extend our evaluation to the AdvBench harmful behavior tasks and the GCG attack method.
