The success of a jailbreak attack is correlated with the model's attention on sensitive words; successful attacks divert attention away from harmful terms.
ABA achieves higher attack success rates (ASR-G >94%) than existing methods by minimizing attention on sensitive words and maximizing attention entropy.
ABD effectively defends against various jailbreak attacks by detecting anomalous attention distributions, achieving the lowest ASR-G in experiments.
The intention disguiser via attention-driven task nesting is a critical component for the success of ABA.
Excessive nesting layers in attack prompts can reduce effectiveness, with an optimal number around 3.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attack can be used to access the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by inducing LLMs to generate the harmful content. And the most common method of the attack is to construct semantically ambiguous prompts to confuse and mislead the LLMs. To access the security and reveal the intrinsic relation between the input prompt and the output for LLMs, the distribution of attention weight is introduced to analyze the underlying reasons. By using statistical analysis methods, some novel metrics are defined to better describe the distribution of attention weight, such as the Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words (Attn_SensWords), the Attention-based Contextual Dependency Score (Attn_DepScore) and Attention Dispersion Entropy (Attn_Entropy). By leveraging the distinct characteristics of these metrics, the beam search algorithm and inspired by the military strategy "Feint and Attack", an effective jailbreak attack strategy named as Attention-Based Attack (ABA) is proposed. In the ABA, nested attack prompts are employed to divert the attention distribution of the LLMs. In this manner, more harmless parts of the input can be used to attract the attention of the LLMs. In addition, motivated by ABA, an effective defense strategy called as Attention-Based Defense (ABD) is also put forward. Compared with ABA, the ABD can be used to enhance the robustness of LLMs by calibrating the attention distribution of the input prompt. Some comparative experiments have been given to demonstrate the effectiveness of ABA and ABD. Therefore, both ABA and ABD can be used to access the security of the LLMs. The comparative experiment results also give a logical explanation that the distribution of attention weight can bring great influence on the output for LLMs.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Model-Editing-Based Jailbreak against Safety-aligned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is there a more stealthy jailbreak attack vector for LLMs that minimizes user involvement by directly modifying internal model structures to bypass safety alignment without input modifications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Targeted Model Editing (TME), a white-box jailbreak method that bypasses safety filters by identifying and removing safety-critical transformations (SCTs) from MLP weight matrices, enabling harmful responses without input modifications while preserving normal model functionality.
papers.conclusion: The work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security via model editing-based jailbreaks and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations for unsafe samples are highly consistent (due to uniform refusal), while activations for safe samples are more variable.
The difference in average activation values between safe and unsafe samples is significantly larger than the variation within unsafe samples.
The overlap rate of activated neurons between safe and unsafe inputs is low (below 25%), indicating distinct processing pathways.
The D-LLM framework, which implements TME, achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% across four open-source LLMs.
The method maintains model performance on standard benchmarks (TruthfulQA, MMLU) after editing, showing preserved functionality.
future_direction: Further unveil the vulnerabilities of D-LLM and provide insights for LLM developers to bolster safety.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed numerous fields by enabling advanced natural language interactions but remain susceptible to critical vulnerabilities, particularly jailbreak attacks. Current jailbreak techniques, while effective, often depend on input modifications, making them detectable and limiting their stealth and scalability. This paper presents Targeted Model Editing (TME), a novel white-box approach that bypasses safety filters by minimally altering internal model structures while preserving the model's intended functionalities. TME identifies and removes safety-critical transformations (SCTs) embedded in model matrices, enabling malicious queries to bypass restrictions without input modifications. By analyzing distinct activation patterns between safe and unsafe queries, TME isolates and approximates SCTs through an optimization process. Implemented in the D-LLM framework, our method achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% on four mainstream open-source LLMs, maintaining high performance. Unlike existing methods, D-LLM eliminates the need for specific triggers or harmful response collections, offering a stealthier and more effective jailbreak strategy. This work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.

papers.title: Pruning for Protection: Increasing Jailbreak Resistance in Aligned LLMs Without Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How does model compression, specifically pruning, affect the jailbreak resistance of aligned large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Moderate pruning using WANDA increases jailbreak resistance in aligned LLMs without fine-tuning, while preserving performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning can improve jailbreak resistance in safety-trained LLMs, but excessive pruning reduces safety, suggesting that careful pruning can aid in deploying safe models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning at 10-30% sparsity improves jailbreak resistance, with peak improvement at 20% sparsity for LLaMA-2 Chat.
The degree of safety improvement correlates with the initial model's safety level; models with more safety training show greater improvement.
Pruned models exhibit sharper attention patterns and are less distracted by jailbreak pretexts.
Pruned models assign higher perplexity to jailbreak constructs, indicating increased sensitivity to out-of-distribution prompts.
Pruning enhances resistance against both manual jailbreak attempts and automated attacks like GCG.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 7-billion parameter models and WANDA pruning; results may not generalize to larger models or other compression techniques.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models
Explore other compression techniques beyond WANDA pruning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of model compression on the way Large Language Models (LLMs) process prompts, particularly concerning jailbreak resistance. We show that moderate WANDA pruning can enhance resistance to jailbreaking attacks without fine-tuning, while maintaining performance on standard benchmarks. To systematically evaluate this safety enhancement, we introduce a dataset of 225 harmful tasks across five categories. Our analysis of LLaMA-2 Chat, Vicuna 1.3, and Mistral Instruct v0.2 reveals that pruning benefits correlate with initial model safety levels. We interpret these results by examining changes in attention patterns and perplexity shifts, demonstrating that pruned models exhibit sharper attention and increased sensitivity to artificial jailbreak constructs. We extend our evaluation to the AdvBench harmful behavior tasks and the GCG attack method. We find that LLaMA-2 is much safer on AdvBench prompts than on our dataset when evaluated with manual jailbreak attempts, and that pruning is effective against both automated attacks and manual jailbreaking on Advbench.

papers.title: Causal Front-Door Adjustment for Robust Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly jailbreak Large Language Models (LLMs) by modeling the internal safety mechanism as an unobserved confounder and using causal front-door adjustment to sever its confounding effect?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, causal jailbreaking framework (CFA2) that models safety mechanisms as unobserved confounders, uses Sparse Autoencoders to isolate task intent, and applies weight orthogonalization to physically sever the confounding link, enabling robust and efficient jailbreaking.
papers.conclusion: CFA2 is an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for jailbreaking LLMs by leveraging causal inference and sparse feature disentanglement to bypass safety guardrails.
papers.key_findings:
CFA2 achieves a state-of-the-art average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 83.68% across four safety-aligned LLMs, significantly outperforming optimization-based baselines.
The method reduces the complex causal marginalization to a deterministic forward pass with O(1) inference complexity, drastically improving efficiency.
CFA2 maintains high stealthiness by preserving natural language fluency in prompts, as evidenced by low perplexity scores.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of sparse representations (via SAE) for precise intervention and the superiority of weight orthogonalization over runtime activation clamping.
The method demonstrates robustness across different model architectures and generation lengths.
papers.limitation: The method requires white-box access to the model for SAE training and direct parameter modification, precluding direct application to closed-source models.
future_direction: Distilling the internal causal insights from CFA2 into black-box prompt optimization strategies to bridge the gap to closed-source models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment mechanisms in Large Language Models (LLMs) often operate as latent internal states, obscuring the model's inherent capabilities. Building on this observation, we model the safety mechanism as an unobserved confounder from a causal perspective. Then, we propose the Causal Front-Door Adjustment Attack (CFA{$^2$}) to jailbreak LLM, which is a framework that leverages Pearl's Front-Door Criterion to sever the confounding associations for robust jailbreaking. Specifically, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to physically strip defense-related features, isolating the core task intent. We further reduce computationally expensive marginalization to a deterministic intervention with low inference complexity. Experiments demonstrate that CFA{$^2$} achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates while offering a mechanistic interpretation of the jailbreaking process.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: ALERT: Zero-shot LLM Jailbreak Detection via Internal Discrepancy Amplification
papers.research_question: How to detect jailbreak attacks in a zero-shot setting where no jailbreak templates are available during training, by amplifying internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot jailbreak detection task and a detector (ALERT) that amplifies internal discrepancies at layer, module, and token levels to identify unseen jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: ALERT demonstrates strong zero-shot detection capability against unseen jailbreak attacks, significantly outperforming existing baselines and satisfying practicality principles for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers (particularly the 3rd and 4th) encode safety-relevant semantics and exhibit large distributional discrepancies.
Gating and context features within the FFN provide stronger zero-shot discriminative signals than hidden states due to decoupled activation responses.
Jailbreak templates exhibit a larger token-level distribution gap from benign and harmful prompts compared to harmful instructions.
ALERT consistently achieves over 90% Accuracy and F1-score in zero-shot detection, outperforming baselines by at least 10% on average.
The proposed amplification mechanisms progressively improve detection performance, with module-wise amplification yielding the largest gain.
papers.limitation: The detector adopts a relatively simple VIB-based design; more advanced designs from generalization and domain adaptation could further improve robustness.
future_direction: Incorporate techniques from generalization and domain adaptation to explicitly reduce the domain gap between harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Explore using gating and context features for jailbreak mitigation through post-training strategies like reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Despite rich safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain highly susceptible to jailbreak attacks, which compromise safety guardrails and pose serious security risks. Existing detection methods mainly detect jailbreak status relying on jailbreak templates present in the training data. However, few studies address the more realistic and challenging zero-shot jailbreak detection setting, where no jailbreak templates are available during training. This setting better reflects real-world scenarios where new attacks continually emerge and evolve. To address this challenge, we propose a layer-wise, module-wise, and token-wise amplification framework that progressively magnifies internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts. We uncover safety-relevant layers, identify specific modules that inherently encode zero-shot discriminative signals, and localize informative safety tokens. Building upon these insights, we introduce ALERT (Amplification-based Jailbreak Detector), an efficient and effective zero-shot jailbreak detector that introduces two independent yet complementary classifiers on amplified representations. Extensive experiments on three safety benchmarks demonstrate that ALERT achieves consistently strong zero-shot detection performance. Specifically, (i) across all datasets and attack strategies, ALERT reliably ranks among the top two methods, and (ii) it outperforms the second-best baseline by at least 10% in average Accuracy and F1-score, and sometimes by up to 40%.

papers.title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in safety alignment, and how can they be addressed with a dual-objective optimization approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DOOR, a dual-objective optimization method that combines robust refusal training and targeted unlearning to improve LLM safety alignment against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: DOOR and W-DOOR improve LLM safety alignment by combining refusal training and unlearning, achieving better robustness against jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
DOOR addresses limitations of DPO by providing a constant learning rate for safe responses, improving refusal learning.
W-DOOR with token-level weighting further enhances robustness by emphasizing critical refusal tokens.
The methods significantly reduce attack success rates across prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
Robustness is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations.
The approach maintains general model utility while improving safety, as shown on benchmarks like HellaSwag.
papers.limitation:
Token-level weighting parameters could be better optimized and stabilized.
Current data augmentation techniques may lead to overrefusal from falsely learned transitions.
future_direction: Optimizing token-level weighting parameters and stabilizing reward designs.
Developing advanced data augmentation techniques to reduce overrefusal.
Investigating robustness of DOOR and W-DOOR to other jailbreak attack types.
papers.abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment

papers.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How is refusal encoded in the latent space of LLMs, and how do adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using sparse autoencoders to identify and causally validate refusal-related features in LLMs, revealing that harm and refusal are separately encoded and that adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal features.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify causal refusal features, revealing the mediation of refusal by harmful features and the suppression mechanism of adversarial jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate feature sets, with harmful features exhibiting a causal effect on refusal features.
Adversarial jailbreaks operate by suppressing specific refusal-related features.
The identified refusal features significantly improve classification on out-of-distribution adversarial examples.
The proposed CosSim+AP method identifies a minimal set of causal features for refusal behavior.
There is a conditional relationship where harmful features upstream trigger refusal features downstream.
papers.limitation:
The small K* may omit additional features relevant to harm and refusal.
The reliance on the refusal direction may not generalize to challenging instructions.
SAEs were trained on base models, not chat models, which may affect interpretability.
future_direction: Training SAEs on chat-model activations to improve feature interpretability and relevance.
papers.abstract: Refusal is a key safety behavior in aligned language models, yet the internal mechanisms driving refusals remain opaque. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study of refusal in instruction-tuned LLMs using sparse autoencoders to identify latent features that causally mediate refusal behaviors. We apply our method to two open-source chat models and intervene on refusal-related features to assess their influence on generation, validating their behavioral impact across multiple harmful datasets. This enables a fine-grained inspection of how refusal manifests at the activation level and addresses key research questions such as investigating upstream-downstream latent relationship and understanding the mechanisms of adversarial jailbreaking techniques. We also establish the usefulness of refusal features in enhancing generalization for linear probes to out-of-distribution adversarial samples in classification tasks. We open source our code in https://github.com/wj210/refusal_sae.

papers.title: AttentionDefense: Leveraging System Prompt Attention for Explainable Defense Against Novel Jailbreaks
papers.research_question: Can system-prompt attention from Small Language Models (SLMs) be used to characterize adversarial prompts for jailbreak detection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AttentionDefense, a method that uses system-prompt attention weights from SLMs to detect jailbreaks, offering an explainable, scalable, and generalizable defense.
papers.conclusion: AttentionDefense improves the explainability, scalability, and generalizability of jailbreak detection by leveraging system prompt attention from SLMs, demonstrating robustness against both known and novel jailbreak attacks.
papers.key_findings:
AttentionDefense (using Phi-2) achieves an F1-score of 0.86 on novel jailbreaks, outperforming text embedding-based classifiers and matching the performance of the much larger GPT-4 detector.
System prompt attention is a more robust and generalizable signal for jailbreak detection than semantic embeddings, performing equally well on known and novel jailbreaks.
Defining the jailbreak mechanism in the system prompt is more critical for high-precision detection than defining the payload.
Fine-tuned models (e.g., Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) may not be good candidates for using latent representations like attention for detection, as safety fine-tuning appears to obscure the signal.
AttentionDefense provides a cheaper alternative to LLM-based detectors, achieving comparable performance with models that are 800 times smaller in parameters.
papers.limitation:
AttentionDefense is anchored by a system prompt; if the system prompt is not well-engineered, the attention weights may not show meaningful differences between benign and malicious prompts.
Any change to the system prompt requires the training data to be regenerated and the classifier retrained.
AttentionDefense inherits constraints of the underlying SLM, such as small context windows.
future_direction: Investigating if system prompt attention can be used for other detector use cases outside of jailbreaks.
Exploring if a similar approach to AttentionDefense can be built using unsupervised learning to measure out-of-distribution detection, removing the requirement for labeled data.
papers.abstract: In the past few years, Language Models (LMs) have shown par-human capabilities in several domains. Despite their practical applications and exceeding user consumption, they are susceptible to jailbreaks when malicious input exploits the LM's weaknesses, causing it to deviate from its intended behavior. Current defensive strategies either classify the input prompt as adversarial or prevent LMs from generating harmful outputs. However, it is challenging to explain the reason behind the malicious nature of the jailbreak, which results in a wide variety of closed-box approaches. In this research, we propose and demonstrate that system-prompt attention from Small Language Models (SLMs) can be used to characterize adversarial prompts, providing a novel, explainable, and cheaper defense approach called AttentionDefense. Our research suggests that the attention mechanism is an integral component in understanding and explaining how LMs respond to malicious input that is not captured in the semantic meaning of text embeddings. The proposed AttentionDefense is evaluated against existing jailbreak benchmark datasets. Ablation studies show that SLM-based AttentionDefense has equivalent or better jailbreak detection performance compared to text embedding-based classifiers and GPT-4 zero-shot detectors.To further validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, we generate a dataset of novel jailbreak variants of the existing benchmark dataset using a closed-loop LLM-based multi-agent system. We demonstrate that the proposed AttentionDefense approach performs robustly on this novel jailbreak dataset while existing approaches suffer in performance. Additionally, for practical purposes AttentionDefense is an ideal solution as it has the computation requirements of a small LM but the performance of a LLM detector.

papers.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning
papers.research_question: How can refusal behavior in safety-aligned language models be ablated without causing collateral damage to core capabilities like math and coding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), a method that cleans refusal vectors by orthogonalizing against capability and style directions, enabling precise ablation of refusal behavior with minimal distribution drift and preserved capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SRA treats refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem, achieving behavioral editing with dramatically reduced drift and preserved capabilities compared to standard methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on wikitext_2_raw and minimal distribution drift.
Standard ablation induces severe distribution drift, while SRA maintains original distribution while achieving low refusal rates.
SRA preserves or improves math and code perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP datasets.
The dirty refusal vector is polysemantic, entangling refusal signals with unrelated linguistic structure and capability circuits.
Cleaning the vector via spectral residualization reduces 'Ghost Noise' damage caused by standard ablation.
papers.limitation:
The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction.
Evaluation limitations include refusal detection being definition-dependent, finite harmful prompt suites, and proxy drift metrics not substituting for comprehensive behavioral evaluation.
future_direction: Automating atom discovery or expanding registries to handle unseen confounds.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models systematically refuse harmful requests. While activation steering can modulate refusal, ablating the raw "refusal vector" calculated from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts often causes collateral damage and distribution drift. We argue this degradation occurs because the raw vector is polysemantic, entangling the refusal signal with core capability circuits and linguistic style. We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA) to distill these steering directions. SRA constructs a registry of independent Concept Atoms representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, then uses ridge-regularized spectral residualization to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a clean refusal direction that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model's semantic geometry. Across five models (Qwen3-VL and Ministral series), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0-2%) with negligible perplexity impact on Wikitext-2 (mean delta PPL approx. 0.02) and minimal distribution drift. Notably, standard ablation on Qwen3-VL-4B induces severe drift (first-token KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate. Using teacher-forced perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP as a high-resolution capability proxy, we show SRA preserves math and code distributions. These results suggest that common "model damage" is often "Ghost Noise," defined as the spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.

papers.title: Efficient Jailbreaking of Large Models by Freeze Training: Lower Layers Exhibit Greater Sensitivity to Harmful Content
papers.research_question: This study investigates the sensitivity of different layers in Large Language Models to harmful content generation and proposes an efficient jailbreak method using freeze training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies lower layers in LLMs as highly sensitive to harmful content generation and introduces the Freeze-Front5-SFT method, which efficiently jailbreaks models by fine-tuning only these critical layers, achieving high attack success rates with reduced computational costs.
papers.conclusion: This study demonstrates that lower layers are critical for jailbreak attacks, and the Freeze-Front5-SFT method offers an efficient approach for both jailbreaking and informing defense strategies, contributing to LLM security research.
papers.key_findings:
Lower layers (first 20%) are highly sensitive to harmful content generation.
Freeze-Front5-SFT achieves an Attack Success Rate of 84.19% and Harm Score of 4.41 with only 1.5 hours training and 169.2 GB GPU memory, outperforming LoRA-based methods in efficiency.
The method generalizes effectively across various model architectures and sizes, including Qwen2.5, Llama3.1, Baichuan2, GLM4, and Mistral.
Training lower layers is more effective for jailbreaking than training higher layers, as shown by higher ASR and Harm Score.
Freeze-Front5-SFT provides a superior balance between jailbreak effectiveness and resource consumption compared to full-parameter fine-tuning and other LoRA methods.
papers.limitation:
Model Generalizability: Findings may not generalize to all LLM architectures, especially those with different layer configurations or attention mechanisms.
Layer Interaction Dynamics: Analysis focused on individual layers without accounting for cross-layer interactions.
Temporal Stability: Experiments did not assess long-term model behavior or jailbreak persistence.
Dataset Scope: Dataset primarily focuses on text-based attacks, leaving multimodal jailbreaks unexplored.
future_direction: Extend analysis to emerging architectures like mixture-of-experts models.
Conduct longitudinal studies of jailbreak persistence.
Develop more sophisticated analysis of cross-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: With the widespread application of Large Language Models across various domains, their security issues have increasingly garnered significant attention from both academic and industrial communities. This study conducts sampling and normalization of the parameters of the LLM to generate visual representations and heatmaps of parameter distributions, revealing notable discrepancies in parameter distributions among certain layers within the hidden layers. Further analysis involves calculating statistical metrics for each layer, followed by the computation of a Comprehensive Sensitivity Score based on these metrics, which identifies the lower layers as being particularly sensitive to the generation of harmful content. Based on this finding, we employ a Freeze training strategy, selectively performing Supervised Fine-Tuning only on the lower layers. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly reduces training duration and GPU memory consumption while maintaining a high jailbreak success rate and a high harm score, outperforming the results achieved by applying the LoRA method for SFT across all layers. Additionally, the method has been successfully extended to other open-source large models, validating its generality and effectiveness across different model architectures. Furthermore, we compare our method with ohter jailbreak method, demonstrating the superior performance of our approach. By innovatively proposing a method to statistically analyze and compare large model parameters layer by layer, this study provides new insights into the interpretability of large models. These discoveries emphasize the necessity of continuous research and the implementation of adaptive security measures in the rapidly evolving field of LLMs to prevent potential jailbreak attack risks, thereby promoting the development of more robust and secure LLMs.

papers.title: JailBound: Jailbreaking Internal Safety Boundaries of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the internal safety decision boundaries within Vision-Language Models be exploited to perform effective jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JailBound, a novel jailbreak framework that identifies and exploits the internal latent safety decision boundary within Vision-Language Models to craft effective adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: JailBound exposes a critical safety vulnerability in VLMs by exploiting their internal latent knowledge, highlighting the urgent need for more robust cross-modal safety alignment mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
JailBound achieves state-of-the-art white-box attack success rates (e.g., 94.38% on LLaMA-3.2) and exceptional black-box transferability (e.g., 75.24% against GPT-4o).
The method demonstrates that VLMs encode safety-relevant information in fusion-layer representations, revealing an implicit safety decision boundary that can be approximated and crossed via adversarial perturbations.
Joint optimization of image and text perturbations guided by the probed boundary is more effective than decoupled unimodal attacks.
papers.limitation:
The work does not extensively explore defenses specifically tailored to this attack vector.
Experiments primarily utilize a fixed set of perturbation budgets; a more fine-grained analysis of the relationship between perturbation magnitude and attack success across diverse model architectures could provide further insights.
future_direction: Developing more generalizable and resilient multimodal defense strategies.
Conducting a more fine-grained analysis of the relationship between perturbation magnitude and attack success across diverse model architectures.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit impressive performance, yet the integration of powerful vision encoders has significantly broadened their attack surface, rendering them increasingly susceptible to jailbreak attacks. However, lacking well-defined attack objectives, existing jailbreak methods often struggle with gradient-based strategies prone to local optima and lacking precise directional guidance, and typically decouple visual and textual modalities, thereby limiting their effectiveness by neglecting crucial cross-modal interactions. Inspired by the Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) framework, we posit that VLMs encode safety-relevant information within their internal fusion-layer representations, revealing an implicit safety decision boundary in the latent space. This motivates exploiting boundary to steer model behavior. Accordingly, we propose JailBound, a novel latent space jailbreak framework comprising two stages: (1) Safety Boundary Probing, which addresses the guidance issue by approximating decision boundary within fusion layer's latent space, thereby identifying optimal perturbation directions towards the target region; and (2) Safety Boundary Crossing, which overcomes the limitations of decoupled approaches by jointly optimizing adversarial perturbations across both image and text inputs. This latter stage employs an innovative mechanism to steer the model's internal state towards policy-violating outputs while maintaining cross-modal semantic consistency. Extensive experiments on six diverse VLMs demonstrate JailBound's efficacy, achieves 94.32% white-box and 67.28% black-box attack success averagely, which are 6.17% and 21.13% higher than SOTA methods, respectively. Our findings expose a overlooked safety risk in VLMs and highlight the urgent need for more robust defenses. Warning: This paper contains potentially sensitive, harmful and offensive content.

papers.title: Jailbreak Instruction-Tuned LLMs via end-of-sentence MLP Re-weighting
papers.research_question: How does re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences affect the safety mechanisms of instruction-tuned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and introduces two white-box jailbreak methods that re-weight MLP neurons to compromise safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and that re-weighting these neurons can effectively jailbreak the models, providing insights for both attack and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences can significantly compromise the safety of instruction-tuned LLMs.
The prompt-specific jailbreak method outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-specific methods and requires less computational time.
The prompt-general jailbreak method is comparable to state-of-the-art approaches and has minimal impact on the model's original capabilities (except for very small models).
The safety mechanism of instruction-tuned LLMs heavily relies on MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences.
The method can also serve as a mechanism interpretability tool to identify MLP neurons strongly correlated with safety.
papers.limitation:
The method is heuristic-driven, making it more of a validation experiment rather than an optimal solution.
The precise role MLP layers play in the safety mechanism and how they impact subsequent generation processes remain open questions.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the safety mechanisms of instruction fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). We discover that re-weighting MLP neurons can significantly compromise a model's safety, especially for MLPs in end-of-sentence inferences. We hypothesize that LLMs evaluate the harmfulness of prompts during end-of-sentence inferences, and MLP layers plays a critical role in this process. Based on this hypothesis, we develop 2 novel white-box jailbreak methods: a prompt-specific method and a prompt-general method. The prompt-specific method targets individual prompts and optimizes the attack on the fly, while the prompt-general method is pre-trained offline and can generalize to unseen harmful prompts. Our methods demonstrate robust performance across 7 popular open-source LLMs, size ranging from 2B to 72B. Furthermore, our study provides insights into vulnerabilities of instruction-tuned LLM's safety and deepens the understanding of the internal mechanisms of LLMs.

papers.title: Eraser: Jailbreaking Defense in Large Language Models via Unlearning Harmful Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreaking attacks in Large Language Models by unlearning harmful knowledge while retaining general capabilities and safety alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Eraser, a jailbreaking defense method that unlearns harmful knowledge via gradient ascent while retaining general knowledge and safety alignment, significantly reducing attack success rates without compromising general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Eraser effectively defends against jailbreaking by unlearning harmful knowledge, maintaining general performance, and enhancing safety alignment, offering a better balance between harmlessness and usefulness compared to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Eraser significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and harmfulness scores for various jailbreaking attacks (AIM, AutoDAN, GCG).
Eraser maintains general capabilities comparable to the base model across multiple benchmarks (e.g., ARC, HellaSwag).
Using random prefixes/suffixes during unlearning (T(·)) enhances defensive capability against jailbreaking.
Unlearning harmful text contributes to defense, but gradient ascent on random token sequences also yields defense at the cost of general performance degradation.
The threshold γ controls the trade-off between defense performance and general capability; a moderate value (e.g., 2) is recommended.
papers.limitation:
Eraser is inefficient as it only defends against specific harmful issues, and enumerating all harmful issues is challenging.
Eraser is only applicable to LLMs that have undergone safety alignment.
future_direction: Future research on jailbreaking defense should focus more on maintaining general capabilities.
More effort is needed to enhance safety alignment so that unlearning methods like Eraser can become an alternative to technologies like RLHF.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking attacks can enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to bypass the safeguard and generate harmful content. Existing jailbreaking defense methods have failed to address the fundamental issue that harmful knowledge resides within the model, leading to potential jailbreak risks for LLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel defense method called Eraser, which mainly includes three goals: unlearning harmful knowledge, retaining general knowledge, and maintaining safety alignment. The intuition is that if an LLM forgets the specific knowledge required to answer a harmful question, it will no longer have the ability to answer harmful questions. The training of Erase does not actually require the model's own harmful knowledge, and it can benefit from unlearning general answers related to harmful queries, which means it does not need assistance from the red team. The experimental results show that Eraser can significantly reduce the jailbreaking success rate for various attacks without compromising the general capabilities of the model. Our codes are available at https://github.com/ZeroNLP/Eraser.

papers.title: SafeLLM: Unlearning Harmful Outputs from Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models by unlearning harmful outputs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeLLM, a token-level unlearning framework that integrates dynamic detection, FFN activation tracing, and constrained optimization to suppress harmful outputs in LLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving general performance.
papers.conclusion: SafeLLM achieves irreversible forgetting of harmful behavior, significantly reducing jailbreak attack success rates without degrading general performance, offering a scalable and proactive defense for LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
SafeLLM significantly reduces Attack Success Rates (ASR) across jailbreak benchmarks compared to baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
It maintains general performance on benign datasets such as OpenBookQA and TruthfulQA after unlearning.
SafeLLM enables irreversible forgetting of harmful behaviors by targeting FFN substructures responsible for harmful token generation.
The framework demonstrates robustness to unseen adversarial prompts through feature-driven generalization.
Ablation studies show that dynamic fusion weights and adaptive trust-region bounds optimize the safety-utility trade-off.
future_direction: Advance unlearning techniques to tackle broader challenges related to fairness, transparency, and adversarial threats in multi-modal LLMs.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks pose a serious threat to the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) by crafting adversarial prompts that bypass alignment mechanisms, causing the models to produce harmful, restricted, or biased content. In this paper, we propose SafeLLM, a novel unlearning-based defense framework that unlearn the harmful knowledge from LLMs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities. SafeLLM employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) dynamic unsafe output detection using a hybrid approach that integrates external classifiers with model-internal evaluations; (2) token-level harmful content tracing through feedforward network (FFN) activations to localize harmful knowledge; and (3) constrained optimization to suppress unsafe behavior without degrading overall model quality. SafeLLM achieves targeted and irreversible forgetting by identifying and neutralizing FFN substructures responsible for harmful generation pathways. Extensive experiments on prominent LLMs (Vicuna, LLaMA, and GPT-J) across multiple jailbreak benchmarks show that SafeLLM substantially reduces attack success rates while maintaining high general-purpose performance. Compared to standard defense methods such as supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization, SafeLLM offers stronger safety guarantees, more precise control over harmful behavior, and greater robustness to unseen attacks. Moreover, SafeLLM maintains the general performance after the harmful knowledge unlearned. These results highlight unlearning as a promising direction for scalable and effective LLM safety.

papers.title: DELMAN: Dynamic Defense Against Large Language Model Jailbreaking with Model Editing
papers.research_question: How to defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models in a dynamic, precise, and minimal way during the deployment phase?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DELMAN, a dynamic defense mechanism that directly edits a minimal set of model parameters to neutralize harmful behaviors from jailbreak attacks while preserving the model's utility on normal tasks.
papers.conclusion: DELMAN demonstrates how token-level direct model editing can effectively enhance LLM safety against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance, offering a practical solution for post-deployment protection.
papers.key_findings:
DELMAN significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across multiple jailbreak attack types and datasets, often to 0%.
DELMAN preserves or even improves model utility on general-purpose and downstream tasks compared to baseline defenses.
DELMAN's edits are transferable across different harmful behaviors and datasets due to overlapping representations of harmful tokens.
DELMAN supports consecutive edits without interfering with previous modifications, enabling dynamic defense updates.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to general-purpose LLMs, leaving applicability to domain-specialized models and larger-scale models unexplored.
DELMAN relies on GPT-4 for harmful token extraction and context generation, introducing dependency on external models and potential cost barriers.
The stability of consecutive edits, though preliminarily validated, needs deeper analysis to assess potential performance drift over extended deployment.
future_direction: Investigate more efficient methods for harmful token identification, e.g., using a minimal set of tokens to cover the majority of harmful scenarios.
Explore the application of DELMAN to domain-specific LLMs and VLMs to validate its generalizability across different domains and modalities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely applied in decision making, but their deployment is threatened by jailbreak attacks, where adversarial users manipulate model behavior to bypass safety measures. Existing defense mechanisms, such as safety fine-tuning and model editing, either require extensive parameter modifications or lack precision, leading to performance degradation on general tasks, which is unsuitable to post-deployment safety alignment. To address these challenges, we propose DELMAN (Dynamic Editing for LLMs JAilbreak DefeNse), a novel approach leveraging direct model editing for precise, dynamic protection against jailbreak attacks. DELMAN directly updates a minimal set of relevant parameters to neutralize harmful behaviors while preserving the model's utility. To avoid triggering a safe response in benign context, we incorporate KL-divergence regularization to ensure the updated model remains consistent with the original model when processing benign queries. Experimental results demonstrate that DELMAN outperforms baseline methods in mitigating jailbreak attacks while preserving the model's utility, and adapts seamlessly to new attack instances, providing a practical and efficient solution for post-deployment model protection.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks via Layer-specific Editing
papers.research_question: How do large language models respond to harmful prompts, and how can we enhance their resilience against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Layer-specific Editing (LED), a defense method that identifies and edits safety layers in early LLM layers to align them with safe responses, improving jailbreak resistance while maintaining helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: LED effectively defends LLMs against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers, maintaining helpfulness on benign prompts.
papers.key_findings:
Early safety layers are crucial for defending against harmful prompts; pruning them causes LLMs to generate harmful responses.
Jailbreak attacks do not affect all layers; some layers still decode to refusal tokens.
LED effectively reduces attack success rate across various jailbreak attacks.
LED maintains model helpfulness on benign prompts.
Editing both safety layers and additional middle layers yields the best trade-off between safety and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted in a wide range of real-world applications. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have shown that LLMs are vulnerable to deliberately crafted adversarial prompts even when aligned via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or supervised fine-tuning. While existing defense methods focus on either detecting harmful prompts or reducing the likelihood of harmful responses through various means, defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks based on the inner mechanisms of LLMs remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate how LLMs response to harmful prompts and propose a novel defense method termed \textbf{L}ayer-specific \textbf{Ed}iting (LED) to enhance the resilience of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Through LED, we reveal that several critical \textit{safety layers} exist among the early layers of LLMs. We then show that realigning these safety layers (and some selected additional layers) with the decoded safe response from selected target layers can significantly improve the alignment of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Extensive experiments across various LLMs (e.g., Llama2, Mistral) show the effectiveness of LED, which effectively defends against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance on benign prompts. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ledllm/ledllm}.

papers.title: Beyond Surface Alignment: Rebuilding LLMs Safety Mechanism via Probabilistically Ablating Refusal Direction
papers.research_question: How can we make large language models more robust against jailbreak attacks by rebuilding their safety mechanisms via probabilistically ablating the refusal direction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DeepRefusal, a safety alignment framework that forces LLMs to dynamically rebuild refusal mechanisms from jailbreak states by probabilistically ablating the refusal direction across layers and token depths during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: DeepRefusal bridges the gap between surface-level alignment and robust internal defense by forcing models to rebuild safety mechanisms from jailbreak states, offering a principled way to enhance LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
DeepRefusal reduces attack success rates by approximately 95% across various jailbreak attacks.
It effectively defends against prefilling attacks and refusal direction attacks, including transfer attacks.
The method maintains model capabilities (e.g., on MMLU, GSM8k) with minimal performance degradation.
It shows strong robustness to unseen jailbreak attacks and generalizes across languages without language-specific modifications.
Using a single static refusal direction with harmful prefix augmentation provides the best balance of robustness and capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method is fundamentally dependent on refusal directions within the model, so extending it to multimodal models requires first extending these refusal directions to the multimodal context.
Variations in model size, architecture, and training data can influence defense performance, and the inclusion of high-quality data to mitigate over-refusal is crucial.
future_direction: Extending DeepRefusal to multimodal scenarios.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks pose persistent threats to large language models (LLMs). Current safety alignment methods have attempted to address these issues, but they experience two significant limitations: insufficient safety alignment depth and unrobust internal defense mechanisms. These limitations make them vulnerable to adversarial attacks such as prefilling and refusal direction manipulation. We introduce DeepRefusal, a robust safety alignment framework that overcomes these issues. DeepRefusal forces the model to dynamically rebuild its refusal mechanisms from jailbreak states. This is achieved by probabilistically ablating the refusal direction across layers and token depths during fine-tuning. Our method not only defends against prefilling and refusal direction attacks but also demonstrates strong resilience against other unseen jailbreak strategies. Extensive evaluations on four open-source LLM families and six representative attacks show that DeepRefusal reduces attack success rates by approximately 95%, while maintaining model capabilities with minimal performance degradation.

papers.title: GradSafe: Detecting Jailbreak Prompts for LLMs via Safety-Critical Gradient Analysis
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak prompts for LLMs be detected using safety-critical gradient analysis without requiring further training or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: GradSafe is a method that detects jailbreak prompts by analyzing gradients of safety-critical parameters in LLMs, outperforming finetuned models like Llama Guard without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: GradSafe examines safety-critical parameters of LLMs to identify unsafe prompts, demonstrating that it can outperform finetuned models without requiring additional training on the original LLM.
papers.key_findings:
GradSafe-Zero, applied to Llama-2 without further training, outperforms finetuned Llama Guard and online moderation APIs on ToxicChat and XSTest benchmarks.
GradSafe-Adapt, using logistic regression on gradient features, shows improved adaptability with minimal training data, matching Llama Guard's performance with only 20% of data.
Identifying safety-critical parameters via gradient similarity gaps reduces noise and improves detection performance compared to using all gradients.
GradSafe works effectively with aligned chat models (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat-hf) but not with pretrained models without alignment, highlighting the importance of safety alignment.
Compliance responses like 'Sure' or rejection responses like 'I'm sorry' activate safety-critical parameters better than neutral responses, enhancing detection.
papers.limitation:
The method is only evaluated on Llama-2 and may not generalize to other LLMs.
GradSafe provides a binary safety assessment and does not offer fine-grained classification for specific threat categories.
future_direction: Developing fine-grained classification for specific threat categories.
Extending the method to other base LLMs beyond Llama-2.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) face threats from jailbreak prompts. Existing methods for detecting jailbreak prompts are primarily online moderation APIs or finetuned LLMs. These strategies, however, often require extensive and resource-intensive data collection and training processes. In this study, we propose GradSafe, which effectively detects jailbreak prompts by scrutinizing the gradients of safety-critical parameters in LLMs. Our method is grounded in a pivotal observation: the gradients of an LLM's loss for jailbreak prompts paired with compliance response exhibit similar patterns on certain safety-critical parameters. In contrast, safe prompts lead to different gradient patterns. Building on this observation, GradSafe analyzes the gradients from prompts (paired with compliance responses) to accurately detect jailbreak prompts. We show that GradSafe, applied to Llama-2 without further training, outperforms Llama Guard, despite its extensive finetuning with a large dataset, in detecting jailbreak prompts. This superior performance is consistent across both zero-shot and adaptation scenarios, as evidenced by our evaluations on ToxicChat and XSTest. The source code is available at https://github.com/xyq7/GradSafe.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: When Smiley Turns Hostile: Interpreting How Emojis Trigger LLMs' Toxicity
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether emojis can enhance toxicity generation in LLMs and how to interpret this phenomenon.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emojis can effectively trigger toxicity generation in LLMs across languages and models, and interprets this via tokenization and representation gaps, linking it to data pollution in pre-training corpora.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the risk of emojis in triggering toxicity and call for safety alignment that goes beyond literal languages.
papers.key_findings:
Emojis can effectively trigger toxicity generation in LLMs across mainstream languages, more effective than textual counterparts.
Tokenization disparity provides emojis a heterogeneous semantic expression channel, causing an internal representation gap that makes LLMs less sensitive to harmfulness.
Data pollution exists in pre-training corpora with emoji-related entries, which may facilitate malicious intent understanding and tolerance of toxicity generation.
Emojis can enhance existing jailbreak methods.
Models can recognize malicious intent expressed by emojis but still generate toxic content.
future_direction: Improving safety alignment to handle non-literal languages like emojis
papers.abstract: Emojis are globally used non-verbal cues in digital communication, and extensive research has examined how large language models (LLMs) understand and utilize emojis across contexts. While usually associated with friendliness or playfulness, it is observed that emojis may trigger toxic content generation in LLMs. Motivated by such a observation, we aim to investigate: (1) whether emojis can clearly enhance the toxicity generation in LLMs and (2) how to interpret this phenomenon. We begin with a comprehensive exploration of emoji-triggered LLM toxicity generation by automating the construction of prompts with emojis to subtly express toxic intent. Experiments across 5 mainstream languages on 7 famous LLMs along with jailbreak tasks demonstrate that prompts with emojis could easily induce toxicity generation. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct model-level interpretations spanning semantic cognition, sequence generation and tokenization, suggesting that emojis can act as a heterogeneous semantic channel to bypass the safety mechanisms. To pursue deeper insights, we further probe the pre-training corpus and uncover potential correlation between the emoji-related data polution with the toxicity generation behaviors. Supplementary materials provide our implementation code and data. (Warning: This paper contains potentially sensitive contents)

papers.title: The Laminar Flow Hypothesis: Detecting Jailbreaks via Semantic Turbulence in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can jailbreaks in large language models be detected by analyzing the variance in layer-wise semantic trajectories?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Laminar Flow Hypothesis and Semantic Turbulence, a zero-shot metric for detecting jailbreaks in LLMs by analyzing internal latent trajectories, and demonstrates its ability to diagnose safety architectures.
papers.conclusion: Semantic Turbulence serves as an effective jailbreak detector and diagnostic tool for categorizing safety architectures in LLMs, based on the Laminar Flow Hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic Turbulence effectively discriminates between benign and adversarial inputs with statistical significance.
Qwen2-1.5B exhibits a 75.4% increase in turbulence under attack, indicating a conflict-based safety mechanism.
Gemma-2B shows a 22.0% decrease in turbulence, suggesting a reflex-based refusal mechanism.
Two distinct safety signatures are identified: conflict-based (high turbulence) and reflex-based (low turbulence).
The metric is lightweight, real-time, and requires no auxiliary training, making it suitable for deployment.
future_direction: scalability to larger models
robustness against adaptive attacks
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become ubiquitous, the challenge of securing them against adversarial "jailbreaking" attacks has intensified. Current defense strategies often rely on computationally expensive external classifiers or brittle lexical filters, overlooking the intrinsic dynamics of the model's reasoning process. In this work, the Laminar Flow Hypothesis is introduced, which posits that benign inputs induce smooth, gradual transitions in an LLM's high-dimensional latent space, whereas adversarial prompts trigger chaotic, high-variance trajectories - termed Semantic Turbulence - resulting from the internal conflict between safety alignment and instruction-following objectives. This phenomenon is formalized through a novel, zero-shot metric: the variance of layer-wise cosine velocity. Experimental evaluation across diverse small language models reveals a striking diagnostic capability. The RLHF-aligned Qwen2-1.5B exhibits a statistically significant 75.4% increase in turbulence under attack (p less than 0.001), validating the hypothesis of internal conflict. Conversely, Gemma-2B displays a 22.0% decrease in turbulence, characterizing a distinct, low-entropy "reflex-based" refusal mechanism. These findings demonstrate that Semantic Turbulence serves not only as a lightweight, real-time jailbreak detector but also as a non-invasive diagnostic tool for categorizing the underlying safety architecture of black-box models.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense
papers.research_question: Can models learn to enhance their own safety without relying on external validators by leveraging their internal confidence (entropy) signals?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that aligned models have an entropy gap between safe and unsafe responses and introduces SIRL, which uses this entropy as an intrinsic reward signal for self-alignment without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: Effective safety alignment can emerge from models' own confidence signals, paving the way for autonomous AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned models exhibit lower entropy (higher confidence) when generating safe refusals compared to harmful content.
SIRL achieves high defense success rates (over 89%) against diverse jailbreak attacks.
SIRL preserves or improves general capabilities (mathematics, coding, conversation) while enhancing safety.
SIRL is data-efficient, requiring only 15,000 unlabeled prompts.
SIRL generalizes to novel jailbreak techniques.
papers.abstract: Ensuring Large Language Model (LLM) safety remains challenging due to the absence of universal standards and reliable content validators, making it difficult to obtain effective training signals. We discover that aligned models already possess robust internal safety beliefs: they consistently produce high-confidence refusals to harmful requests while exhibiting high entropy when generating potentially dangerous content. This entropy gap reveals an untapped signal--models intrinsically "know" when to refuse. We introduce Safety Instincts Reinforcement Learning (SIRL), which transforms this internal confidence into a self-generated reward signal, eliminating dependence on external validators or human annotations. SIRL teaches models to trust their safety instincts by reinforcing low-entropy refusal behaviors. Evaluated on Llama and Qwen models, SIRL maintains 89%+ Defense Success Rates (DSRs) against 20+ jailbreak methods, from static prompts to adaptive attacks. Using only 15,000 unlabeled prompts, SIRL surpasses resource-intensive supervised methods while preserving performance on mathematics, coding, and conversation benchmarks.
